## Problem

Your organisation ships AI code. That means notebooks, fine-tune
scripts and demo repos that read model-provider API keys — and the
documented failure mode is one `OPENAI_API_KEY = "sk-..."` pasted into
a shared notebook, committed, and forgotten. On Kailash's manifest this
is Layer ATTACK's a-01-ai-recon surface: trufflehog (the native secret
scanner, A-1 primary + C-8 secondary) carries the detector engine,
while the org-scan/crawler probes frame the shared-compute and
model-hub scope where those keys leak. As the administrator you own
the hunt *inward* — your own repos, your own notebooks — before
someone else runs it outward.

## Solution

Scan the git scope first (history included — a key removed from HEAD
still lives in the objects), then the filesystem scope for the
notebooks that never got committed:

```bash
# 1. What the manifest declares for the A-1 recon surface
kailash list --category a-01-ai-recon
kailash info trufflehog       # -> A-1 primary + C-8 secondary, ATLAS, OWASP

# 2. The org sweep (verified results only — see Discussion for why):
trufflehog github --org=<your-org> --results=verified
#    exclude archived repos from the sweep:
trufflehog github --org=<your-org> --exclude-archived

# 3. One repo, full history, JSON for the tracker:
trufflehog git https://github.com/<your-org>/<repo> --results=verified --json

# 4. The un-committed surface (CI workspaces, shared notebooks,
#    scratch checkouts):
trufflehog filesystem /srv/notebooks /home/<user>/scratch

# 5. The model-hub + shared-compute scopes need hand work today: the
#    pre-#210 first-party probe rows (org-scan,
#    notebook-crawl) were PHANTOM-upstream — claimed kailash-os repos
#    never created — removed by the os#210 audit; the names ride the
#    [os#210 registry](https://github.com/kailash-os/kailash-os/issues/210).
#    Interim honest path: enumerate the org's hub surface with the HF
#    public API (no auth for public entities) and review notebook
#    scopes with trufflehog filesystem (step 4) against the checkout
#    of your shared workspace.
```

Expected output shape (abridged, shapes not transcripts):

```
🐷🔑🐷  TruffleHog. Unearth your secrets. 🐷🔑🐷

Found verified result 🐷🔑
Detector Type: <provider, e.g. AWS / OpenAI>
Decoder Type: <PLAIN|Base64|...>
Raw result: <redacted-in-display key material>
Line: <n>
Commit: <sha>
File: <path>
Email: <committer>
Repository: <url>
Timestamp: <when the credential landed in history>
```

Then the response — and the order is not negotiable:

```bash
# 7. REVOKE FIRST. Every confirmed live key is burned before anything
#    else happens: rotate it at the provider, confirm the old value
#    is dead, THEN clean the repo (history rewrite is a separate,
#    later problem — see the discipline note in Discussion).
#    (provider-side rotation — no command here; do it in the
#     provider's console while the finding is fresh)

# 8. Record the finding + disposition against your own tracker
#    (the JSON output from step 3 is the machine-readable half;
#     the timestamp/commit/file triple is what your report cites)

# 9. Put the posture back: keys out of repos entirely
#      model API keys live at runtime from ~/.config/kailash/keys/
#      (the OS secrets posture — store paths are world-readable)
```

## Discussion

- **`--results=verified` is the whole discipline:** trufflehog does
  discovery, classification, *validation* and analysis — of 800+
  detector types — and validation is the step that separates a live
  credential from a string that looks like one. A verified finding is
  an active danger; an unverified match is a hypothesis. The upstream
  demo output above IS the verified-result shape. AI-provider
  coverage in the detector set is real and checkable at the pin:
  the `pkg/detectors` tree at main carries `openai`, `anthropic`,
  `huggingface`, `deepseek`, `gemini`, `groq`, `openrouter`, `xai`,
  `replicate`, `elevenlabs`, `deepgram`, `assemblyai`, `alibaba`
  among its ~900 detector packages — verify your specific providers'
  detectors at your lock before you rely on them.
- **Revoke-first is not negotiable — and the ATLAS mapping is why.**
  The manifest rows map trufflehog to AML.T0004 + AML.T0055 (Search
  Victim-Owned Websites / Unsecured Credentials), OWASP LLM02 (2026) /
  LLM02+LLM07 (v2) — the pre-#210 notebook-crawl probe's mapping rode the
  removed phantom row (os#210)
  the attack this hunt imitates is one that does not clean up — it
  uses the key. Any cleanup you do before revocation is time the
  live credential keeps working. History rewriting (git filter-repo
  class) comes after rotation, because the objects still exist even
  after the rewrite on any fork or clone you do not control.
- **The inward scope is the administrator's part of an ATTACK row:**
  the category is offensive, but the hunt against your OWN org is the
  defender-validation case the responsible-use statement names —
  written authorisation is still the standing requirement, and this
  recipe's scope (your org, your notebooks) is exactly the
  authorised-work shape. Running the same engines against someone
  else's scope is the A-1 recon lane's business, not this recipe's.
- **The probes were aspirational-only:** the pre-#210
  The org-scan + notebook-crawl probe rows claimed first-party
  upstreams that never existed — REMOVED by the os#210 audit; their
  surfaces were manifest-contract descriptions and now ride the
  [os#210 registry](https://github.com/kailash-os/kailash-os/issues/210).
  The no-fake-surfaces rule that governs this book demanded this
  purge — a PENDING row cannot survive an upstream that never existed.
- **Posture after the burn:** the OS-side secrets posture puts model
  API keys at runtime from `~/.config/kailash/keys/` (sops-nix for
  declarative secrets) precisely because Nix store paths are
  world-readable — the recurrence prevention half of this recipe is
  configuration, not vigilance.
- **When the results say nothing:** an all-clear is only as good as
  the detectors at your lock. Record the detector set (the manifest
  row pins the scanner version) with the sweep date — this recipe
  re-runs at every release window otherwise, per the book's upkeep
  rule.
